title: Severe period pain is not normal: doctors explain endometriosis risks and long diagnosis delays
excerpt: Gynaecologists say debilitating menstrual pain can signal endometriosis — a condition affecting 190 million women worldwide that takes an average of eight to ten years to diagnose.
body:
• Severe, recurrent period pain that disrupts daily life is not normal and can be a sign of endometriosis, gynaecologists warn.
  • Endometriosis — tissue resembling the uterine lining growing outside the uterus — affects about 1 in 10 women of reproductive age, or 190 million women globally.
  • Diagnosis typically takes eight to ten years; symptoms are often dismissed as normal period pain, and India's fragmented referral system adds further delay.
  • A close family member with the condition raises risk, with genetics interacting with hormonal, immune and environmental factors.

Severe period pain is not always normal. Gynaecologists say debilitating menstrual pain can be a sign of endometriosis — a chronic inflammatory condition that affects roughly one in ten women of reproductive age worldwide, yet often takes the better part of a decade to diagnose.

Context & Background

Endometriosis occurs when tissue resembling the endometrium, the uterus lining, grows outside the uterus. It affects an estimated 190 million women globally and can cause intense pelvic pain, fatigue, depression, anxiety and infertility. Symptoms include severe menstrual cramps, pain during intercourse, persistent pelvic pain, pain during bowel movements or urination around menstruation, and later, difficulty conceiving.

The diagnostic journey is long. Research puts the average delay at eight to ten years; in the UK it is more than nine years, according to researchers. Symptoms often begin in adolescence but are dismissed as "normal period pain", and ultrasounds typically do not pick up the small early lesions — meaning it is often only the most severe cases that get diagnosed, researchers at Bournemouth University note.

In India, the journey is harder still. The Sen Times reported that India's pluralistic health system and lack of referral systems force women to navigate multiple providers, including traditional healers and alternative practitioners, increasing complexity and financial burden.

Impact & Analysis

Genetics plays a real but partial role. Dr Jyotsna Suri, head of gynaecology and obstetrics at Delhi's Safdarjung Hospital, told The Sen Times that endometriosis is "not simply a genetic disorder but a complex disease resulting from the interaction of genetic, hormonal, immune and environmental factors." Women with a close family member affected may have a higher risk, she said, adding that epigenetic changes — which alter how genes are expressed without changing the DNA sequence — may also matter.

Large genetic studies back that complexity. A Nature Genetics study comparing more than 60,000 women with endometriosis against 700,000 without identified 42 genetic regions linked to the condition — more than double the previously known 17. Many of the implicated genes involve the immune system, inflammation and cell movement. The study also found a shared genetic basis between endometriosis and other chronic pain conditions such as migraine and back pain, suggesting sensitisation of the central nervous system. A New Scientist report on recent research noted three genetic regions detected only in genomes of people with African ancestry, and links between endometriosis-related genes, inflammation and cardiovascular disease.

The treatment implication: current therapies focus on hormonal pathways, since oestrogen makes lesions grow, bleed and inflame surrounding tissue. But if inflammation drives symptoms and wider health problems, researchers say existing anti-inflammatory drugs could become part of the answer.

"Importantly, severe period pain should never be dismissed as something a woman simply has to live with. Pain that disrupts daily life, pain during intercourse, persistent pelvic pain or difficulty conceiving warrants medical evaluation."

— Dr Jyotsna Suri, Head of Gynaecology and Obstetrics, Safdarjung Hospital, Delhi

Dr Bindu Bajaj, also at Safdarjung Hospital, said endometriosis should be considered when menstrual pain is severe, recurrent or progressively worsening — particularly when routine painkillers provide little relief, or when pain affects school, work, sleep or social activities. She stressed that awareness among adolescents and families is equally important, since painful periods can begin early and symptoms may worsen over time. Pain that disrupts daily life, pain during intercourse, persistent pelvic pain or difficulty conceiving warrants medical evaluation — early recognition can shorten the diagnostic journey and help preserve reproductive health.

Diaspora Angle

Endometriosis does not respect borders, and diaspora women face the same pattern of delayed diagnosis. For women who have spent years being told their pain is normal, the message from doctors is direct: pain that disrupts daily life deserves a gynaecological evaluation, not endurance.

What's Next

Researchers say richer genetic data puts medicine "in a much better position to be able to speed up" diagnosis, as the University of Queensland's Professor Grant Montgomery put it — and opens new drug targets beyond hormonal treatments. Until then, awareness remains the fastest intervention: recognising severe, worsening or treatment-resistant period pain as a medical problem, not a fact of life.
